newsitem.title: USA: Local gov'ts should note investing experience - SEC.
newsitem.headline: Local gov'ts should note investing experience - SEC.

text.p: A top SEC lawyer urged state and local finance officers on Sunday to tell their broker-dealers if they are inexperienced in investing in government securities.

Catherine McGuire, chief counsel for the Securities and Exchange Commission's division of market regulation, said the strategy is important in light of the National Association of Securities Dealers' new suitability rules for the sale of government securities, including derivatives, to institutional buyers.

"It is imperative that government finance officers be knowledgeable about what they are investing in, and to state clearly if they are not," McGuire told finance officers meeting here this week for the Government Finance Officers Association's annual conference.

That is because the new rules require dealers - before they sell to institutional buyers like localities - to decide whether the buyer is capable of evaluating investment risks independently, McGuire said. If not, then the seller must decide whether the sale is a suitable one, under the rules, she said.

"You should make clear if you are in fact relying on the broker dealer because that is the best way to invoke the (new rule's) suitability obligations," McGuire said. "In other words, you just can't fake it."

McGuire warned localities not to become complacent now that NASD has developed new standards for dealers. "These are regulations and you can use them to recover (losses). You can sue your broker dealer, but that takes a long time."

"The first line of defense must be risk management ... at home," McGuire said. She urged officers to clarify their investment objectives and to spell them out to securities salespeople, even if that means laying bare their investment portfolios. She also recommended "good monitoring and internal audits."
Susan Anderson, city treasurer for Austin, Texas, had sobering remarks about how Texas localities are grappling with new state standards for local government investing.
The requirements were triggered by massive losses by a state college whose portfolio manager invested heavily in collateralized mortgage obligations, she said.

The state now bars local officials from purchasing any investments unless salesmen certify that they have thoroughly reviewed the locality's investment policy and that they have "reasonable procedures and controls in effect" to guard against imprudent investments by the client, Anderson said.

She said a lot of securities firms refused to sign certifications, "crippling" smaller government investors. She said firms are justifiably concerns about "weighted" average maturity limits in a lot of the investment plans being developed by cities and counties.
But Anderson said GFOA of Texas and other groups are developing a two-part certification that most securities firms are warming up to.

Public funds would pledge to have investment policies in place and not stray from them. Broker dealers would promise to get a copy of a locality's investment policy, understand it, and have controls in place to implement it, Anderson said.

Van Sayler, senior vice president of Raymond James & Associates, Inc. in St. Petersburg, Fla., said his firm is experimenting with having its dealers "certify compliance with a list of appropriate securities."
He recommended that GFOA develop three certification program for finance officers that want to learn about government and agency securities, mortgage bonds and corporate bonds.
